summary.text: Algae are a large and diverse group of photosynthetic organisms that excludes the land plants.
They range from microscopic single-celled microalgae to seaweeds, multicellular macroalgae that may grow up to 50 metres long.
Most algae live in water, especially the sea, and most are photoautotrophs, the main primary producers of aquatic ecosystems.

facts.label: Field of study
facts.value: Phycology, from the Greek for seaweed

facts.label: Longest forms
facts.value: Seaweeds up to 50 metres (160 ft) long

facts.label: Fossil filaments
facts.value: Dated to 1.6 to 1.7 billion years ago

facts.value: Thousands of years old, strong in East Asian food cultures

facts.label: Oxygen making
facts.value: They produce oxygen by splitting water molecules

items.prompt: A tree is photosynthetic and lives in sunlight, yet it is not called an alga. Why?

options.label: Trees cannot photosynthesise like algae do
Algae exclude the land plants, which are called embryophytes
Algae must be single-celled
Algae must live in the ocean

items.explain: Algae are photosynthetic organisms that exclude the land plants (embryophytes).

items.prompt: Is it true that everything studied as algae photosynthesises?

options.label: No, some lost their chlorophyll or became heterotrophs or parasites
Yes, otherwise it could not be called algae
Yes, though colourless ones do it only in the dark
Yes, colourless ones use a different pigment

items.explain: Many non-photosynthetic protists are included in the study of algae, such as colourless species that lost chlorophyll in evolution, and some unicellular algae became heterotrophs or parasites.

items.prompt: Algae are mostly aquatic. Can any live away from open water?

options.label: No, all algae need open water at all times
Yes, all algae can, with no moisture needed
Only large seaweeds with holdfasts can manage it
A few species tolerate dry land, given some moisture

items.explain: Some exceptional species tolerate dry terrestrial habitats, such as soil, rocks, or caves, although they still need enough moisture to become active.

items.prompt: Chlorophytes, rhodophytes and glaucophytes got primary chloroplasts straight from cyanobacteria. Where did diatoms and brown algae get theirs?

options.label: Indirectly, from endosymbiont red algae or green algae
They have no chloroplasts and feed on other cells
Directly from cyanobacteria, like the others
They built their own chloroplasts from scratch

items.explain: Diatoms, cryptomonads, euglenoids and brown algae have secondary chloroplasts derived indirectly from endosymbiont red or green algae.

items.prompt: Biologists tracing the ancestors of land plants look to which algae?

options.label: Kelps, which are the longest brown algae
Charophytes, the most complex algae
Cyanobacteria, which are prokaryotes
Diatoms, which are single cells

items.explain: The most complex forms are found among the charophyte algae, in a lineage that eventually led to the higher land plants.

items.prompt: A student says all algae descend from one ancestral alga. What is wrong with that?

options.label: Algae are younger than land plants
Algae descend from land plants
Algae are polyphyletic, with several separate evolutionary origins
Only seaweeds count as algae, and they come from fungi

items.explain: Algae are polyphyletic as they have multiple evolutionary origins.

paragraphs.heading: What algae are
paragraphs.text: Algae is a name for a huge and varied collection of living things that use photosynthesis. The land plants are left out of the group. Algae run from single cells so small you need a microscope, called microalgae, up to seaweeds built from many cells that can stretch to 50 metres. Most of them, though, are single cells with no roots, leaves or stems.

paragraphs.heading: Where they live
paragraphs.text: Most algae live in water, and above all in the sea. Many drift as plankton, moved passively by the water around them, while some large seaweeds hold on to the bottom with an anchor called a holdfast. Freshwater kinds include Spirogyra, which grows in threads, and the stoneworts, which look like grass. A few unusual species manage on dry ground, in soil, on rocks or in dark caves, but they still need some moisture before they become active.

paragraphs.heading: How they make a living
paragraphs.text: Most algae feed themselves through photosynthesis, and they are the chief primary producers of life in water. Their main light-catching pigment is chlorophyll a. Their photosynthetic machinery descends from cyanobacteria and gives off oxygen by splitting water. Some are mixotrophs, which combine photosynthesis with taking in nutrients from outside. A few single-celled algae have become heterotrophs or parasites, getting all their energy from outside sources.

paragraphs.heading: Many origins, one name
paragraphs.text: Algae do not form one family on the tree of life. They are polyphyletic, which means they arose several separate times in evolution. Red, green and grey algae got their chloroplasts directly from cyanobacteria living inside them. Brown algae, diatoms and some others got theirs second-hand, from a red or green alga taken inside. The group even spans cyanobacteria, which are prokaryotes, alongside photosynthetic protists, which are eukaryotes.

paragraphs.heading: From simple to complex
paragraphs.text: Only the red and brown algae and some green ones build three-dimensional bodies made of many cells. Brown, red and green algae have each gone further still, with fully separate tissues, and some brown kelps reach 50 metres. The most complex algae are the charophytes, the line that eventually gave rise to land plants. Land plants differ in one key way: their female organs wrap the young embryo in protective layers of cells, which is why they are called embryophytes.

paragraphs.heading: Ancient and useful
paragraphs.text: Algae have a long history. Fossil threads of algae from the Vindhya basin date to 1.6 to 1.7 billion years ago. People have farmed seaweed for thousands of years, with deep roots in East Asian cooking. Today algae are also grown for cattle feed, to clean up pollution, to turn sunlight into fuels and industrial chemicals, and for medicine and science.

paragraphs.heading: Where the name comes from
paragraphs.text: The word alga is Latin for seaweed, and it keeps that meaning in English. Its most likely source is alliga, meaning binding or entwining. The study of algae is usually called phycology, from a Greek word for seaweed.
